clue.text: She has a game with the team leader

parts.note: bridge is the card game

indicators.note: the leader of the team is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A woman takes part in a sport alongside the captain of her side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' is the definition: any woman's name fits it, here BRIDGET.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridget is a girl's name, so the pronoun can stand for a woman so called.

clue.text: It's literally at the reader's finger-tips

definitions.text: It's literally at the reader's finger-tips

parts.words: It's literally at the reader's finger-tips
parts.note: the figure of speech is meant literally: raised dots read by touch

explanation.definitionFit: The raised-dot writing system for blind people is read by running the fingers over it.

clue.text: Americans booked when abroad? Not guilty!

explanation.surface: Americans arrested overseas protest their innocence.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Twain's travel book The Innocents Abroad follows Americans touring Europe; and the blameless are free of guilt.

clue.text: Measures bits of fish

explanation.definitionFit: A gill is a quarter-pint liquid measure; and fish breathe through these organs.

clue.text: Depravity? Trade union impolite about mine

indicators.note: about means one word goes round the other

parts.note: rude means impolite
a pit is a coal mine

explanation.surface: Is it wicked for the union to be rude about the colliery?
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts RUDE around PIT, the mine, after TU.
explanation.definitionFit: Turpitude is base wickedness, a formal word for moral depravity.

clue.text: Drink with the Corps is paramount

parts.note: to sup is to drink in sips
REME, the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps

explanation.surface: A toast with the regiment matters above all else.
explanation.walkthrough: REME is the British Army's corps of Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: Supreme means highest in rank, which is what being paramount says.

clue.text: Sound of cane to make us smart

explanation.surface: The swing of the cane, meant to make us sting.
explanation.definitionFit: The whistling noise a cane makes through the air; and in British slang, fashionable or posh.

clue.text: Perry worried about censor expressing a wish

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters wrap round the other piece
worried suggests agitation, so the letters of Perry are disturbed

parts.note: Cato the Elder, the Roman censor

explanation.surface: Perry frets about the censor, hoping for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' rearranges PERRY to PRERY, and 'about' wraps it round CATO, the famous Roman censor.
explanation.definitionFit: Precatory is a legal term for words of request or entreaty, as in a will.

clue.text: How to get out of the Geneva Declaration

indicators.note: of means the letters are part of the words that follow

explanation.surface: How to escape the terms of an international agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across GenEVA DEclaration; 'How to' and 'the' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: To evade is to escape or avoid something by cleverness.

clue.text: Turned out Green entered river upside down

indicators.note: entered means one piece goes inside the other
in a down clue upside down means the word river's name is read bottom to top

parts.note: the Dee is a British river
vert is green in heraldry

explanation.surface: A Green politician falls into a river and comes up the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upside down' turns DEE to EED, and 'entered' puts VERT, heraldic green, inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Everted means turned inside out, a technical word in anatomy.

clue.text: Girl, a beginner, makes record of the year

parts.note: Ann is a girl's name
L is for learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A young novice writes up the year's events.
explanation.walkthrough: L is the learner, from the L-plate that British learner drivers display.
explanation.definitionFit: The singular of annals: a chronicle entry setting down one year's events.

clue.text: Trouble in Eritrea, the heartless keep repeating

indicators.note: trouble suggests disorder, so the letters of Eritrea and the trimmed word are stirred up
heartless asks for the middle letter of the word the to be removed

explanation.surface: Conflict in the African state, with the callous going on and on about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' takes the H out of THE, leaving TE; that joins ERITREA as the fodder signalled by 'Trouble'.
explanation.definitionFit: To reiterate is to say again and again, which is to keep on repeating.

clue.text: Reluctant to include poor Mick's craftsman

indicators.note: one word is made to include the other, so the rearranged letters go inside

parts.note: loth is an old spelling of loath, unwilling

indicators.note: poor suggests something badly made, so the letters of Mick's are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone unwilling to take on an inept Mick as an apprentice tradesman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges MICKS to CKSMI, and 'to include' puts that inside LOTH, unwilling.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who makes and mends locks and keys is a skilled artisan.

clue.text: Air raid warning comes later perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the word later is one possible arrangement of other letters

explanation.surface: The siren sounds after the bombers have already struck, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges LATER; 'comes' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An alert is a signal warning of danger, such as an air raid siren.

clue.text: No end of an important role for birds

indicators.note: no end of asks for the last letter of the name to be cut off

parts.note: Ernest, the name Jack assumes in Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest

explanation.surface: An actor has no end of a major part to play among the birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an important role' plays on Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest, where the hero poses as Ernest; 'No end of' drops its last letter T.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernes are sea eagles, a crossword staple among birds of prey.

clue.text: Being doubtful, sadly accepts one pound

indicators.note: sadly suggests things going wrong, so the letters of accepts are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
L is the pound sign, from libra

explanation.surface: Unsure of himself, a man reluctantly takes a single pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges ACCEPTS to SCEPTCA; then I and L follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Sceptical means inclined to doubt or question, the British spelling of skeptical.

clue.text: Like Edward V Uncle's beginning to wonder, somehow

indicators.note: somehow says the letters come together in some other way
beginning asks only for the opening stretch of the word, its first three letters

parts.note: the word uncle

explanation.surface: A boy king's uncle starts to wonder about something, as Richard did with Edward V.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning' keeps UNC from UNCLE; 'somehow' rearranges UNC with WONDER. Edward V, one of the Princes in the Tower, was never crowned.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward V reigned briefly in 1483 but disappeared before any coronation, so he was a king never crowned.

clue.text: A tower of strength on the farm

definitions.text: A tower of strength on the farm

parts.words: A tower of strength on the farm
parts.note: tower is read as one who tows: a powerful animal hauling a cart

explanation.definitionFit: A heavy draught horse is bred to pull loads, so it tows with great strength.

clue.text: What's a bird at in Nice ? Give us the wink

indicators.note: in means the pieces are placed inside the other word

parts.note: the French city, its name as written
a tit is a small bird

explanation.surface: What is a bird up to on the Riviera? Wink at us.
explanation.walkthrough: TIT and AT go 'in' NICE; 'What's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To nictitate is to blink, as with the third eyelid of a bird.

clue.text: Does Turk see me maybe as D'Artagnan ?

indicators.note: maybe suggests the words Turk see me could be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A Turk wonders whether he looks like Dumas's hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges TURK and SEE ME; 'Does' and 'as' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: D'Artagnan is the young Gascon who joins Dumas's royal guardsmen in The Three Musketeers, so he is an example of one.

clue.text: Weller upset over quarrel, the dog

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means the name is turned to read upward

parts.note: Sam Weller, Mr Pickwick's servant in Dickens
a tiff is a petty quarrel

explanation.surface: Weller is upset over an argument about the dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Sam Weller is Pickwick's servant in Dickens; 'upset' turns SAM to MAS, and 'over' places it above TIFF in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A mastiff is a large, powerful breed of guard dog.

clue.text: Speedy finish by German eight in this boat

indicators.note: the finish of speedy is its closing letter

parts.note: acht is German for eight

explanation.surface: A fast German rowing eight comes home in a racing craft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finish' takes the last letter of 'Speedy'; ACHT is German for eight. 'eight' looks like a rowing crew, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A yacht is a sailing or pleasure vessel, the kind of craft the clue points to.

clue.text: A lush spot down under to the south

indicators.note: in a down clue down under means the word spot is placed beneath the rest

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A drinker finds a place in Australia to the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down under' looks like Australia, but in a down clue it puts SPOT below TO and S.
explanation.definitionFit: A tosspot is an old word for a drunkard, someone who habitually drinks to excess.

clue.text: Polish associate is without money for rent

indicators.note: without in the old sense of outside: one word sits around the other

parts.note: spit, from the phrase spit and polish
L is the pound sign, standing for money

explanation.surface: A friend from Poland has no cash to pay the landlord.
explanation.walkthrough: Spit goes with polish in 'spit and polish'; 'without' means outside, so SPIT surrounds L, the pound. 'rent' is the noun, a tear, not a payment.
explanation.definitionFit: A rent is a tear or rip in cloth, which is a split.

clue.text: Languish in Asia Minor

explanation.surface: Someone wilting away in Turkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Lydia Languish is the romantic heroine of Sheridan's The Rivals; and Lydia was an ancient kingdom in western Anatolia.

clue.text: Sea urchins feature nothing inside, anyway

annotationWithheld.why: Sea urchins feature nothing inside, anyway (9): the parse is CHIN+O in an anagram ('anyway') of SIDE, reading the one printed word 'inside' as 'in' (indicator) plus 'side' (fodder); a leaf cannot quote part of a word
annotationWithheld.clue: Sea urchins feature nothing inside, anyway

clue.text: Record order to come in

explanation.definitionFit: To enter is to write something into a register; and to come into a room or place.

clue.text: Pearl may be found in northern area

parts.note: an acre is a unit of area

explanation.surface: A gem might turn up in the north of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be found in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Nacre is mother-of-pearl, the lustrous layer that also forms a pearl.

clue.text: It shows many in the country a high spot

indicators.note: in means one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: India, taken as the country
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a large number
a tor is a rocky hill top, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A guidebook marks lots of the nation's peaks.
explanation.walkthrough: C (a hundred, so 'many') goes 'in' INDIA, then TOR, a hill, follows; a tor is a rocky peak on English moors.
explanation.definitionFit: An indicator is a gauge or pointer whose job is to display a reading.

clue.text: This knife — how does it grab you?

explanation.surface: A man brandishes a blade and asks how you like it.
explanation.walkthrough: A clasp-knife is a folding knife; the second half plays on the slang 'how does it grab you?'
explanation.definitionFit: A clasp-knife has a blade that folds into the handle; and to clasp is to grip or seize.

clue.text: What more flesh made Falstaff

parts.note: Falstaff in Henry IV Part 1 says that having more flesh than another man he has more frailty

explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's fat knight claims his extra weight makes him weaker in will, more open to temptation.

clue.text: Eg fire or heater

explanation.definitionFit: Fire was one of the four classical substances of nature; and the heating coil in a kettle or stove is its working part.
